items.title: Task-Efficient Agent Evaluation Using Cached Traces
items.summary: Efficient benchmarking estimates a system's full benchmark performance from a small number of task executions. Standard approaches rely solely on the binary correctness of executions from a collection of already-evaluated reference systems. An agentic system, however, produces a rich trace for each execution that can reveal substantially more about its capabilities. Leveraging this information requires useful trace representations. We propose representing a trace by extracting a structured summary of it with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. These representations preserve correctness- and task-related signal while minimizing the presence of system identity-, model family- and harness-related signals that dominate raw trace embeddings. Given this representation for each task execution from all reference systems, we construct low-dimensional representations of the systems and predict a new system's score from its position among the reference systems. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, augmenting an item-response model with this geometry-based prediction reduces mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-4}$) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-3}$), respectively, when provided a single random executed task. Further, given access to the full set of reference systems, our approach dominates baselines for any given number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.

items.title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
items.summary: Skills let language agents reuse experience across tasks as natural-language documents. Recent work evolves skills from interaction, but existing methods have limitations when skills evolve online. Prior methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories collected over many tasks. Some then adopt the new skill without any check, which can degrade the skill over time. Others keep it only if it improves performance on a held-out validation set, which is too slow and costly to run after every update. We introduce EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that mitigates skill degradation at low latency and cost. We first run the agent iteratively to build pools of skills and score each skill on a private test set to obtain utility labels. We pair the skills and use rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector is trained on the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill. At deployment it decides in a single forward pass, which is significantly faster than evaluation on the private test set. Compared with adopting every new skill, EvoGuard improves success by 11.0% on ALFWorld, 5.9% on ScienceWorld, and 2.7% on LiveCodeBench.

items.title: On Turn-Level Best-of-N Sampling for Scaling LLM Agents
items.summary: In this work, we evaluate a simple inference-time scaling approach based on \textit{turn-level best-of-N sampling} (\method) for large language model (LLM) agents on complex, long-horizon tasks. We instantiate this using a \textit{generator-selector} framework with two LLMs; at each turn, a \emph{generator} model generates $N$ candidate actions and a \emph{selector} model selects one of them, which is then executed in the environment. This paper is closely related to the work of \cite{zainullina2025guided} who used critic models for guided search at inference time. Different from their work, we evaluate if off-the-shelf, open-weight LLMs can be effective at comparing different candidate actions directly. Experiments on long-horizon terminal tasks show that \method can lead to significant performance improvements, both in terms of accuracy (5--10\%) and consistency across repeated attempts. Analysis of agent trajectories reveal a shift in agent behaviour towards desirable patterns such as reduction in number of attempts to solve the task, improved task instruction following, debugging and testing.

items.content_excerpt: In the last 30 days, Spawn shipped 77,000 substantial changes. That's about 108 an hour, around the clock. We're a team of ten. The work is done by what we call the fleet, a team of permanent AI agents that each own a part of the company, from the engine to finance to bug triage. We spent $3.1 million on tokens last month, which makes us one of Anthropic's biggest customers. Even without the free Opus 5.5 we give our creators, we'd still be in their top 250. My first thought was that we were doing something wrong. So I had chats with some of my friends who run the biggest companies and startups to figure out how we could possibly be spending more than them. We weren't doing anything wrong, we just think about AI very differently. Most companies run big human teams that use AI, and we run a small human team alongside a big team of agents. To figure out what we were doing differently, I compared notes with a researcher at Anthropic. They talk to a lot of customers. They said Spawn is the one that works most like Anthropic. A lot of other founders wanted to understand how we think about this, so I've collected my ideas and learnings from the last year and written them down here for you. Since Fable came out, we've spent a large part of this year rediscovering how to build products from first principles. We now ship 500x more than we did 6 months ago. To give you an idea of the scale I'm talking about, we shipped 77k (substantial) changes to players in the last 30 days. That's an average of 108/hr to players. We spent $3.1 million on tokens to do it. Most people run agents in Claude Code, short-lived and focused on one task. Ours are different, and we call them the fleet. Each one is permanent, has a name and a memory of what it has done, has real permissions in our systems, makes commitments, and owns an area of the company like the engine, Savi, ops, finance, bug triage or deploys. Each uses swarms of helper agents to get through a massive amount of work, and most days the fleet births 1,000s of them. The five of us also work with our modified Claude Code directly, on bigger, more ambitious projects that need closer steering or hands-on experimenting. items.title: Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes
items.summary: Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:introducing kinference an open source inference control plane for vllm and kuber
items.content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . items.title: Maggie Appleton: Agentic Coding Has Outgrown the Text Box
items.summary:
Agentic coding has outgrown the text box. Maggie Appleton, staff research engineer at GitHub Next, argues that walls of CLI output and AGENTS.md files serve coding agents far better than the humans steering them. She walks through Chopin, the GitHub Next prototype where background agents turn a team's planning chat into a structured plan, and makes the case for agents that prompt you instead of waiting to be prompted.

What we cover:
– Why text-heavy agentic coding tools favor agents over humans
– Boundary objects: what AGENTS.md, skill files and MCP servers get right and wrong
– Multiplayer planning with coding agents in GitHub Next's Chopin
– Human-to-agent handoffs, formal verification and spec-driven development
– Why software quality is rising, not falling, with coding agents
– Which roles still matter: PMs, designers and engineers

items.title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

items.title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks
items.summary: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.

items.title: llm 0.37
items.summary:
Release: llm 0.37

There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes.

I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra, plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna.

LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2, which can embed text, audio, images, and video.

A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes!

This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix.

So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721, ac1982, Allen Flux, Bian Yuhan, Bishop Kammeraad, Chen Yufeiyang, Christopher Krah, Ethan Stoner, Jiachen Xie, Olamide Faniyan, Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu, nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release!

items.title: New context engineering challenges in late 2026
items.summary: LangChain CEO Harrison Chase shares insights into the biggest harness engineering challenges with the emergence of proactive agents.
items.story_key: story|title:new context engineering challenges in late 2026
items.content_excerpt: It feels like everyone is converging on the same agent architecture: an LLM, running in a loop, calling tools, running in a sandbox. Claude Code - perhaps the first high profile manifestation of this - came out over a year and a half ago. Deep Agents , our agent harness, launched over a year ago. This pattern has been building for a while. There’s nothing bad with that convergence per se, but it has led to a sentiment among some AI engineers that I’ve talked to recently that “all the hard problems are solved” or “there’s no new AI engineering problems to solve”. When people express this sentiment, I think they are largely talking about the context engineering practices we do to make agents work. And to some extent they are right - there are a lot of standard-ish context engineering solutions we’ve all arrived at: The good news (for context engineering aficionados like myself) is that I think we’re seeing a step function change in agent capabilities, or at least how they are being used. Specifically, over the past few months every agent builder I’ve chatted with has been thinking about proactive, always on, goal-oriented agents . The core of this agent shares a lot of similarities with coding agents, but there are a set of new challenges as well. I highlight a few below. We (at LangChain, and in the industry) don’t necessarily have solutions (or at least, general solutions) for these, so thinking about these has been the most fun I’ve had in a while! How to be proactive without being annoying : These proactive agents run in the background and either listen to event feeds or are woken up with heartbeats. On one hand, they need to be able to push things to the user - that creates a sense of helping. On the other hand, if you push too many notifications to the user, you risk overwhelming them. Calibrating this to be a delightful experience (not too much, not too little) is still a hard context engineering challenge! Memory : Memory for agents has been something we’ve talked with builders about for a while. Memory systems end up having two parts: the underlying data structure and an intelligence layer (agent) around the data. The data structures are often pretty simple ( files , a single string). The hardest part of the intelligence layer is figuring out what to remember. items.title: Uber Builds MCP Gateway to Govern Access to 800+ Servers and 5,000+ AI Agent Tools
items.summary:
Uber has built an MCP Gateway to standardize how AI agents discover and invoke internal services across more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools. The gateway separates tool registration from runtime execution and includes automated API discovery, access controls, sensitive data redaction, incremental tool discovery through Omni MCP, and response filtering.

By Leela Kumili

items.title: claude-code v2.1.318
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session
  • Added assume_role on mantle upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
  • Added an effort option to a mod's $.model.fork, so a quick side job can run at low whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent
  • Added the date a stored claude.ai sign-in ends to claude auth status (loginExpiresAt) and to claude -p JSON results (credential_expires_at)
  • Added a one-line stderr warning to claude -p text output, starting 10 days before a stored claude.ai sign-in ends
  • Fixed --continue sometimes losing the earlier conversation after a malformed tool call's retries ran out (regression in 2.1.314)
  • Fixed macOS sessions with many running Bash commands stalling while memory grew
  • Fixed permission prompts being answered by keys typed just after sending a message, or before a slow prompt appeared
  • Fixed /logout, claude auth logout and claude mcp remove reporting success, and changes to trust, consent or MCP settings being dropped with no word, when the config file could not be updated on a shared network home directory
  • Fixed jobs exiting with Not logged in when another terminal or host signs in again to the same account and organization on the same home
  • Fixed claude mcp add and remove writing the config without its lock: they now wait for it or exit 1, though another job's save can still replace a saved server
  • Fixed claude plugin commands exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed claude plugin validate passing a custom-named marketplace file that claude plugin marketplace add rejects
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers that exit on the version probe being re-probed on every start; a server that dies in under 3s for its own reason is also pinned to the legacy handshake for 7 days
  • Fixed sessions being refused at startup by an allowedProviders list that another login on the same machine had stored
  • Fixed idle compaction replacing a conversation with a reply that was not a summary
  • Fixed the "Now using usage credits" notice reappearing about every 30 seconds while a background subagent is running
  • Fixed custom slash commands that fail, or that only Claude can invoke, printing nothing in claude -p and SDK sessions
  • Fixed claude -p and Agent SDK sessions reporting success when an API error cut off a reply while a mod hooked turn.step
  • Fixed a message sent right after a model change still running after Stop in headless sessions: Stop now cancels or stops it as it would a queued message
  • Fixed a deleted session transcript being re-created with its last prompt when an idle non-interactive session exited
  • Fixed claude remote-control hosts, the background daemon and self-hosted runners failing to start new sessions (spawn ENOENT) after an update or version cleanup removed the binary of a still-running process
  • Fixed a running Claude Code process owned by another user (for example one left by sudo claude) being treated as dead by version cleanup, which could delete its binary
  • Fixed /remote-control showing a session as available after a failed connection
  • Fixed /design revoke reporting success when the request failed with a 404
  • Fixed a shell command approved after a self-hosted runner or cloud session restart running in the session's start folder, not the folder it was asked in; if that folder can't be entered, it is not run
  • Fixed Claude not being told when an approved connector tool was unavailable after a cloud session restart
  • Fixed cloud sessions being stopped in the middle of a turn when the service refuses uploads for several minutes
  • Fixed variables a Setup hook writes to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE not reaching the Bash tool in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed the iPhone app showing a cloud session's turn as finished while it kept running, after a response was cut off at a tool call or a refused image or document was removed
  • Fixed a restarted session re-sending a message that failed with an API error, ahead of the newer message waiting behind it
  • Fixed a restarted session dropping its interrupted turn when the restart came right after Claude read a large image or retried a tool call
  • Fixed every connection failing when the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file is empty, not PEM, or starts with a damaged certificate: readable certificates are now used, with a warning on stderr
  • Fixed workflows re-running finished agents when resumed after a usage limit
  • Fixed /mcp in cloud sessions counting tools the model can't use; a server's row now shows how many of its tools are available
  • Fixed a duplicate notification when Claude left the status field out of a PushNotification call
  • Fixed the error for a too-large image in a request with more than 20 images always saying the limit was 2000px; it now shows the API's limit
  • Fixed the runtime in background shell details not updating while the dialog is open
  • Fixed a mod's turn.step hook making a stopped reply finish as a success in headless runs
  • Fixed retention cleanup leaving a home that only runs claude -p with no ~/.claude.json backup: it now takes a fresh backup before deleting the last good one
  • Fixed the stored login being replaced by an empty file when a network home directory has no room left for data but still takes new files
  • Fixed tokens from setup-token being refused at start on machines with forceLoginOrgUUID, when the token belongs to a permitted organization
  • Fixed non-interactive launches replacing a ~/.claude.json that isn't valid JSON with defaults; the start now fails, says how to restore the file, and leaves it as is (#87551)
  • Fixed an empty ~/.claude.json with no backup being reported as corrupted; Claude Code now starts as it does when the file is missing
  • Fixed the restore command printed for a damaged or missing ~/.claude.json naming an empty or cut-off backup, or failing on a read-only file
  • Fixed the sign-in failure when a stored claude.ai login reaches its time limit: it now says so, and in claude -p names claude auth login and claude setup-token
  • Improved how ~/.claude.json, settings files and the stored login survive saves on shared network home directories: they are less often deleted, briefly emptied or replaced by a near-empty or older copy
  • Improved sessions on network file systems to look again when the configuration file is wrongly reported as missing, so fewer start without your MCP servers and trusted folders
  • Improved MCP tool errors: a call made before the tool is loaded now returns its input schema
  • Improved the reliability of git commits and pull request creation when the Bash tool runs macOS's built-in /bin/bash
  • Improved "Ask your admin for more usage" in the usage limit menu to send the request in one step
  • Improved how fast remote sessions reconnect after a pause or sleep
  • Improved You should know toasts to say "try again" instead of "press 2", which only works in the terminal
  • Improved auto-update reliability: a brief network failure while verifying a release is now retried right away instead of waiting for the next check
  • Improved unattended runs (claude -p, SDK apps) to stop rewriting ~/.claude.json on every run when nothing in it changed
  • Changed Claude Code to no longer install or update the IDE extension when started in an IDE terminal; use /ide from an outside terminal or your editor's extensions view
  • Changed subagents to stop instead of switching models when "Switch models when a message is flagged" is set to "Ask each time"
  • Changed background subagents to move a shell command to the background after 3 minutes on all providers, so the prompt cache doesn't expire while it runs
  • Changed subagent progress summaries on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, or with telemetry off: on a cold prompt cache, one can now wait up to 5 minutes for the subagent's pending response
  • Changed what a mod attaches at prompt.submit to stay in the user's turn rather than go out as a system message
  • Changed deniedMcpServers URL entries to also block Anthropic-provided servers whose upstream URL matches, and connectors in cloud sessions and on self-hosted runners, where the session is given the connector's own URL; otherwise deny a connector by name
  • Changed the /permissions rule details, built-in rules and delete confirmation views to use the standard dialog; pressing Ctrl+C twice there now goes back or cancels instead of quitting
  • Changed /claude-api managed-agents-onboard to give a new agent's built-in tools, and a quickstart template's MCP tools, the auto permission policy ("Judge risky actions") by default, matching the Claude Console; say "run without asking" to opt out
  • Removed the 2.1.288 fix that kept the model's earlier thinking when resuming a conversation started on 2.1.286 or earlier; that thinking can now be dropped
  • Gateway: Added a log warning when the Google access token from a federation (external_account) credentials file is about to expire
  • Gateway: Improved the log hints about listen.trusted_proxies: they now say to list only a proxy that adds the connecting address to X-Forwarded-For itself
  • Gateway: Improved the warning when AWS CountTokens fails on Amazon Bedrock: it says Claude Code, not the gateway, counts after the 501, and points at IAM only when AWS denies access
  • Self-hosted runner: Added CLAUDE_RUNNER_SPAWN_REASON to the orchestrator's spawn-runner hook environment: why Anthropic sent the request (e.g. runner_lost, resumed); unset when none was sent
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a startup warning when --release-idle-session-min is the last argument with no value (still ignored) or has a value of only spaces (still read as 0)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the orchestrator's log lines: ok session=… now prints at every log level on stdout (was debug only, stderr) with reason=… after jti=…, and nack session=… ends its fields with reason=… after retryable=…; update scripts that match retryable=true: or retryable=false:
  • Remote Control: Fixed a misleading "spawn error: ENOENT" when a session's working folder is missing; the error now names the folder
  • Remote Control: Improved the title a fork of a terminal fork is created with when the app doesn't set one: "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed a window whose sign-in the organization's settings refuse starting a new Claude Code process in the background every minute
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long word in the chat panel's error banner pushing its close button out of view
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in screen to show what Claude Code printed when its sign-in status check fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a No repository option: a cloud session on an Anthropic-hosted environment can now start without picking a repository
  • [Cloud sessions] Added the usual Chrome names to cloud sessions, so tools other than Playwright can find the built-in Chromium through google-chrome and CHROME_PATH
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a New session button to the card shown when a cloud session's environment was deleted, where the message box is hidden
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed reading GitHub Actions logs in cloud sessions: gh run view --log and gh api log requests now get the log in most environments, not an unreachable redirect
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved most Create PR failure messages in cloud and Remote Control sessions: they now give the reason or a link to GitHub instead of saying Try again
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed connector search results to tell Claude that the search covers only part of the connector directory
  • [Remote Control] Fixed side-by-side checkouts of one repository looking identical in the environment menu's Remote Control rows; each now shows its own folder name
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed keyboard focus and screen reader announcements in Claude Tag admin setup; pressing Escape in the connect form no longer also closes the Add dialog
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review analytics page to retry once after a server or network failure, then show a Try again banner instead of empty cards
